rows.claim: The conditional construction expresses certainty, not uncertainty or contingency, just as laʿalla does not express divine anxiety.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four stages are existence before birth, earthly life, earthly death, and resurrection; 40:11 similarly speaks of dying and living twice.
rows.anchor: The four stages mentioned here are before birth, during earthly life, earthly death, and resurrection.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the initial dead state as material existence in the body, in the parents’ loins, or as dust of the earth.
rows.anchor: understood either as one’s “existence” in the material stuff of the body, literally in the loins of one’s parents or the dust of the earth

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The alternative is an unremembered or unknown state: Arabs call something dead when its traces are effaced and it is no longer mentioned or remembered.
rows.anchor:
or “remembered” (
madhkūr, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both readings refer to our nonexistence before worldly life.
rows.anchor: before our life in this world.

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿArabī
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabī understands pre-earthly lifelessness as nonmanifestation within God’s Knowledge, not ordinary nothingness; life first gives form to what eternally exists in that Knowledge.
rows.anchor: Someone like the Sufi mystic IbnʿArabī (d. 638/1240) would understand the “lifelessness” of our pre-earthly condition to be a state of nonmanifestation within God’s Knowledge

words: خَلَقَ لَكُم مَّا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ جَمِيعًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God created the things on earth for human beings; related passages include 16:5, 16:13, and 26:166.
rows.anchor: For God’s creation of things for human beings, see also 16:5; 16:13; 26:166.

words: خَلَقَ لَكُم مَّا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ جَمِيعًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creation-for-humanity theme connects with God making creation subservient to people in 22:65, 31:20, and 45:13.
rows.anchor: This idea also relates to God’s making creation subservient to human beings as in 22:65; 31:20; 45:13.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istawā is rendered here as turned to and elsewhere as mounted, including in the cited passages.
rows.anchor: Turned to translates the verb istawā, which is also rendered “mounted” in other contexts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seven heavens connect to the six-day creation in 41:12, their being one above another in 67:3, and earths like them in 65:12.
rows.anchor: For the seven heavens, also see 41:12, where the context is the six days of creation; 67:3, in which they are one upon another; 65:12

rows.speaker: Mujāhid
rows.claim: Mujāhid describes the heavens as above one another and the earths as above one another.
rows.anchor: the early Quran commentator Mujāhid (d. 104/722–23) mentions “heavens above one other” and “earths above one another”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another related passage describes the heavens as having levels.
rows.anchor: and 71:15, which also mentions the “levels” of heavens.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalīfah can mean successor or deputy; khalīfat rasūl Allāh, successor or steward of God’s Messenger, was shortened to khalīfah and anglicized as caliph.
rows.anchor: a word that can also mean “successor” or“deputy,” hence khalīfat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here and in 6:165, khalīfah suggests universal human inheritance and responsibility: all people are, in their inner reality, God’s vicegerents.
rows.anchor: In some verses, such as here and 6:165, khalīfah appears to denote a universal human inheritance and responsibility, since all human beings are in their inner reality the khalīfah of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In other passages khalīfah means successor, as in 7:69 for successors after Noah’s people; related references include 7:74, 10:14, 10:73, 27:62, and 35:39.
rows.anchor: In others, the sense of “successor” comes to the fore (e.g., 7:69, which refers to vicegerents

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators derive khalīfah from khalafa, to come after: humans follow other creatures and summarize all grades of being in the human state.
rows.anchor: some commentators say that khalīfah comes from khalafa (“to come after”) and means that human beings come after all creatures and all grades of being are summarized in the human state.

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās’s report identifies Iblīs as al-Ḥārith, a custodian of Paradise and member of the angelic tribe al-ḥinn, created from smokeless fire unlike the angels created from light.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that Iblīs was a member of a tribe of angels called al-ḥinn

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: In the same report, jinn first inhabited earth and shed blood; God sent Iblīs with the al-ḥinn against them, driving them to islands and mountain edges, and Iblīs grew proud of the victory.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that Iblīs was a member of a tribe of angels called al-ḥinn

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: The report says Adam’s clay body remained lifeless for forty years; Iblīs entered and taunted it, threatening to destroy or defy Adam if either gained power over the other.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that Iblīs was a member of a tribe of angels called al-ḥinn

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: In the account, God commands only the angels accompanying Iblīs to prostrate; Iblīs refuses, claiming superiority by age and greatness and contrasting his fire with Adam’s clay.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that Iblīs was a member of a tribe of angels called al-ḥinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran’s other indication of this order of creation is 15:26–27: human beings were made from molded clay and jinn earlier from scorching fire.
rows.anchor: The only other indication in the Quran of such an order of creation is found in 15:26–27

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators accept that jinn inhabited earth before human beings.
rows.anchor: That jinn inhabited the earth before human beings is accepted by many commentators.

words: قَالُوا۟ أَتَجْعَلُ فِيهَا مَن يُفْسِدُ فِيهَا
rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī prefers that God addressed all the angels, rather than only those who fought alongside Iblīs.
rows.anchor: al-Rāzī prefers the opinion that God spoke to all the angels, not only those who warred alongside Iblīs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The specific story details that Iblīs was an angelic-tribe member are unreliable popular narratives; Ibn ʿAbbās would have known 18:50 identifies Iblīs as a jinn.
rows.anchor: since an authority such as Ibn ʿAbbās would have known that the Quran in 18:50 identifies Iblīs as a jinn, not an angel.

words: أَتَجْعَلُ فِيهَا مَن يُفْسِدُ فِيهَا وَيَسْفِكُ ٱلدِّمَآءَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prior jinn violence offers one possible explanation for the angels’ question about placing a corrupt, blood-shedding being on earth.
rows.anchor: It does, however, provide one possible explanation for the angels’ question, Wilt Thou place therein . . . , namely, that they had previous experience with the blood and corruption of the earth’s previous inhabitants.

words: قَالُوا۟ أَتَجْعَلُ فِيهَا مَن يُفْسِدُ فِيهَا
rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators read the angels’ apparently audacious question as wonder at God’s Wisdom, not doubt or concern; they are not alarmed.
rows.anchor: many commentators explain the angels’ apparently audacious question as an expression of wonder on their part, rather than doubt or concern (R). They marvel at God’s Wisdom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The usual theological view is that angels cannot disobey or rebel.
rows.anchor: It is thought that disobedience or any brand of rebelliousness is impossible for angels

rows.speaker: Muʿtazilites
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī notes the Muʿtazilite view that angels can be disobedient.
rows.anchor: the Muʿtazilites believed that angels could be disobedient.

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: An alternate rendering is We glorify Thee while praising Thee.
rows.anchor: Hymn Thy praise and call Thee Holy can also be read, “We glorify Thee while praising Thee” (Z)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The phrase generally means that good will come from humanity despite inevitable bloodshed and corruption, but only God knows what that good is.
rows.anchor: I know what you know not is generally understood to mean that, despite the inevitability of bloodletting and corruption, good things will come of the creation of human beings, but only God knows what they are (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As noted in 2:11–12, corruption can also mean degradation of the natural environment.
rows.anchor: As mentioned in 2:11–12c, such corruption can also refer to the degradation of the natural environment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The thunderbolt is etymologically related to Moses’ swoon and the swoon of heaven and earth at the trumpet blast on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: The thunderbolt, related etymologically to Moses’ swoon (7:143) and the “swoon” of the heavens and earth at the blowing of the trumpet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thunderbolts also punish ʿĀd and Thamūd; the Thamūd were seized by one as they looked on.
rows.anchor: is also a punishment for the ʿĀd and the Thamūd (41:13). The Thamūd’s thunderbolt also seized them as they looked on.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Ṣāʿiqah can also mean a great calamity or destruction, a great cry or noise, fire, or an earthquake.
rows.anchor: It can also refer more generally to a great calamity or destruction, or a great cry or noise, a fire, or an earthquake (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: Some commentators identify this with 7:155: after the calf’s destruction, Moses took seventy chosen Israelites who had worshipped it; their request to see God was followed by a fatal thunderbolt, then Moses prayed and God revived them.
rows.anchor: Some commentators (IK, R) identify this verse with the incident described in 7:155, which would mean that after the destruction of the calf, Moses went up the mountain with seventy of the choicest Israelites

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Other commentators regard 2:55 and 7:155 as separate incidents.
rows.anchor: Others (JJ) consider 2:55 and 7:155 as separate incidents

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Some commentators take no firm position on whether 2:55 and 7:155 describe the same event.
rows.anchor: some take no firm position (R). The word rendered thunderbolt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāʿiqah has a broader range than rajfah, used for the calamity in 7:155, though the two could denote the same event.
rows.anchor: The word rendered thunderbolt (ṣāʿiqah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jahratan means seeing with one’s eyes or publicly; the word can also describe speech.
rows.anchor: means to see with one’s eyes, or simply “publicly.”

words: لَن نُّؤْمِنَ لَكَ حَتَّىٰ نَرَى ٱللَّهَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demand to see God is also cross-referenced with 4:153.
rows.anchor: Cf. 4:153. The thunderbolt, related etymologically to Moses’ swoon

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: One reading says the passage’s partial belief and disbelief refers to violating the Book by expelling fellow Israelites while obeying it by ransoming them.
rows.anchor: ransom, which would be in accord with the Book(Ṭ).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another reading links disbelief to rejecting prophecies of Muhammad’s coming, but the commentary says the context does not imply this.
rows.anchor: Others connect the disbelief in this verse with the prophecies foretelling the coming of the Prophet Muhammad, though this is not implied by the context (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here kufr has the wider sense of rejecting or denying certain truths, not directly denying God’s existence.
rows.anchor: Here the wider sense of kufr, or “disbelief,” as rejection and denial of certain truths comes to the fore, as the lack of belief and faith in part is not a direct disbelief in God’s existence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expulsion and ransom are hypocrisy and immorality, inseparable from a degree of kufr.
rows.anchor: Rather, the expulsion and taking of ransom are acts of hypocrisy and immorality, which are not separable from a certain degree of kufr.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naskh can mean conveying or copying from an original; this could make the Quran a copy of its Preserved Tablet origin, or simply a written copy of a text.
rows.anchor: Naskh, usually translated “abrogation,” has the meaning of conveyance or copying from an original, which could extend to the notion that the entire Quran is a naskh, or “copy” in relation to its origin in the Preserved Tablet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contextual sense of naskh is erasing or obliterating, compared to the sun erasing shadow, wind erasing dust, or age erasing youth.
rows.anchor: The more relevant sense in this context is “to erase” or “to obliterate,” often described as the action that the sun performs on a shadow, the wind upon dust, or even old age upon youth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root n-s-kh also appears for Moses’ tablets’ inscription, God effacing Satan’s work, and recording human deeds.
rows.anchor: The root n-s-kh appears four times in the Quran: in this verse; in 7:154, referring to the inscription of the tablets of Moses; in 22:52, where God effaces the work of Satan; and in 45:29

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Technical naskh is a major concept in Islamic law, theology, and Quran commentary for understanding the relationship among commands and prohibitions in the Quran and Sunnah and their use in law and practice.
rows.anchor: Naskh (“abrogation”) as a technical term is a key concept in the fully developed form of Islamic jurisprudence, theology, and Quranic commentary

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mainstream definition is replacing an earlier legal ruling with one revealed later; the original text remains in the Quran but is no longer legally binding.
rows.anchor: the replacement of one legal ruling (ḥukm

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Islamic legal sciences, abrogation concerns commands and prohibitions, not descriptive matters of metaphysics, ethics, history, God’s nature, or the Hereafter; a ruling determines legal status rather than doctrine.
rows.anchor: As widely understood in the Islamic religious sciences, naskh can occur only in matters of commands and prohibitions, not in descriptive passages relating to metaphysics, ethics, history, the nature of God, or the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abrogation cannot apply to doctrines such as God’s power or the faithful’s reward, nor to accounts of earlier prophets.
rows.anchor: Thus there can be no abrogation of a passage such as God has power over all things

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibitions of murder, theft, and adultery and the command to treat parents kindly are universal and cannot be abrogated.
rows.anchor: Naskh would not apply to commandments so universal as to be irrevocable

rows.speaker: ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah says Quranic commands about suckling were neither acted upon nor retained in the Quran, an example of abrogating both text and ruling.
rows.anchor: A report attributed to the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah, for example, states that there were commands in the Quran relating to suckling that are now neither acted upon nor part of the Quran

rows.speaker: ʿUmar
rows.claim: A report attributed to ʿUmar says a Quranic stoning command is no longer in the text, though the ruling continues; this is the usual example of abrogating text while retaining its ruling.
rows.anchor: In a report attributed toʿUmar, a verse commanding stoning was part of the Quran

rows.speaker: many jurists (IK, R, Ṭ)
rows.claim: Many, perhaps most, jurists hold that stoning for adultery remains in force despite the verse’s absence from the Quran.
rows.anchor: according to many, if not most, jurists; IK, R, Ṭ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is general agreement that a later Quranic ruling can abrogate an earlier Quranic ruling, but scholars differ on whether Sunnah can abrogate Quran or vice versa, and whether scholarly consensus can abrogate Quran or hadith.
rows.anchor: Although it is generally agreed that one Quranic ruling may abrogate another Quranic ruling revealed earlier in time, there has been considerable difference of opinion about other kinds of naskh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars have proposed widely varying counts of abrogated verses: Shah Walī Allāh named five, Ibn al-Jawzī 247, and al-Suyūṭī 21.
rows.anchor: placed the number of abrogated verses at 5

rows.speaker: Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī
rows.claim: A minority view, represented by Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī, denies technical abrogation and says apparent conflicts can be reconciled.
rows.anchor: A minority of scholars, such as Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī (d. 934/1527), have gone so far as to say that abrogation, as a technical concept defined by the mainstream legal tradition, does not actually exist

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naskh must be distinguished from specification, cumulative law, and a ruling’s lost circumstances or effective cause; it matters practically only when legal rulings cannot be reconciled.
rows.anchor: Even among the mainstream upholders of naskh, abrogation must be distinguished from (1) specification, where a verse does not contradict but provides specification regarding the general ruling of another verse

rows.speaker: Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī
rows.claim: Abū Muslim’s minority alternatives are that naskh occurs between religions, with Islam replacing Judaism and Christianity, or that āyah here means miracle.
rows.anchor: A small minority of scholars, such as Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī

rows.speaker: Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī
rows.claim: On the minority miracle reading, āyah may mean a sign such as the Thamūd she-camel, night and day, the Cave Companions, Zachariah’s silence, Jesus, Moses’ hand, Mary and Jesus, destroyed peoples, miracles, creation, or natural signs.
rows.anchor: A small minority of scholars, such as Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nunsīhā can mean abandon or forsake, as in 9:67; God’s forgetting there does not mean failing to remember.
rows.anchor: can also be understood in the sense of“abandoning,” as in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With different voweling, nansaʾahā means defer or delay, describing signs or verses abrogated and those left unchanged.
rows.anchor: this verb can mean literally “defer/delay,”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and others transmit that two men forgot a surah the Prophet had taught them; he called it abrogated and forgotten, supporting the forgetting reading. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: Ibn Kathīr and others mention aḥadīth about two men who used to recite a sūrah

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some commentators say the replacement is easier in worldly matters but more demanding in matters of the next world: easing the night prayer, but imposing Ramadan fasting for greater reward.
rows.anchor: some interpret better than it as an alleviation when it comes to matters of this world and an intensification when it comes to matters of the next world (Q, Ṭ)

words: مِنْ ءَايَةٍ أَوْ نُنسِهَا نَأْتِ بِخَيْرٍۢ مِّنْهَآ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators supply an implied ruling: it is the ruling, not the sign itself, that is better; al-Ṭabarī compares this ellipsis to the omitted love of the calf in 2:93.
rows.anchor: Thus, for some commentators the verse must mean “No [ruling from a] sign do We abrogate . . . ,” so that it is the ruling, not the sign, that is called “better.” Al-Ṭabarī, for example, compares this implied phrase

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Because khayr can mean a good, another interpretation takes the phrase as a good from or on account of the sign.
rows.anchor: depending on the context (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger requested in Abraham’s prayer is realized in 2:151, where the Prophet is described in terms identical to this verse.
rows.anchor: The response to this prayer for a messenger is realized in v. 151, where the Prophet is described in terms identical to those in this verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book is most often understood as the Quran.
rows.anchor: The Book is most often taken to be the Quran

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Wisdom is understood as the Sunnah, the Prophet’s exemplary sayings and actions.
rows.anchor: the Wisdom is understood to be the Sunnah (the exemplary sayings and doings of the Prophet)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Alternatively, Wisdom means knowledge and understanding of religion more generally.
rows.anchor: or more generally knowledge and understanding of the religion (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Book and Wisdom pairing has broader Quranic use, also appearing in connection with Jesus, the Children of Israel, and Abraham’s House.
rows.anchor: although the pairing of the Book and Wisdom has more universal import in the Quran and is also used in connection with Jesus (3:48; 5:110), the Children of Israel (45:16), and the House of Abraham (4:54).
